newsitem.title: INDIA: India Congress chief lashes out at prime minister.
newsitem.headline: India Congress chief lashes out at prime minister.

text.p: The leader of India's Congress party launched a verbal attack on Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Saturday, stepping up pressure on the ruling United Front (UF) coalition ahead of a vote of confidence.

"I do not have any grudge against the United Front, but this man -- the prime minister -- is not only inefficient but communal," the Press Trust of India quoted Congress president Sitara Kesri as saying.

Kesri triggered a political crisis on March 30 when he abruptly announced his party was withdrawing vital support for Deve Gowda's 10-month-old centre-left coalition, and staked a claim to form a fresh government.
Although Congress, with 140 votes in the 542-member lower house of parliament, lacks enough seats to form a majority, it is counting on some of the 15 parties in the United Front to break away.

Kesri's verbal assault on Deve Gowda appeared part of a strategy to drive a wedge in the United Front by focusing criticism on the prime minister while extending an olive branch to the rest of the coalition.
The United Front said it believed both Congress and the ruling alliance wanted to cement forces and settle their differences amicably.

"We, however, regret to note that the Congress president has been indulging in abusive personal attacks repeatedly on the chairman of the United Front and the prime minister of India, which is not in conformity with the dignity of the office of the president of the Indian National Congress," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy said.
Reddy said the United Front remained united and unbreakable.
By calling Deve Gowda "communal", the Congress leader sought to link the prime minister to the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The BJP's opponents accuse it of fanning communal tensions by favouring India's Hindu majority at the expense of minority Moslems.
Vicious electoral opponents, the United Front and Congress were driven together after inconclusive general elections last year by fear of the BJP.
With 162 deputies, the BJP is the single largest party in the lower house of parliament, and it held power for 12 days last May before it failed to muster enough support to win a vote of confidence.
"He (Deve Gowda) behaves nicely with the BJP people but arrogantly with the Congressmen," Kesri said.
The BJP has said it would like mid-term elections, which opinion surveys indicate would benefit the right-wing party.
But politicians say it would prefer to go to the polls with Deve Gowda, not Kesri, as prime minister, and does not want Congress to have a chance to form a fresh government.

Those preferences have stirred speculation that the BJP could abstain in the vote of confidence set for April 11, handing victory to Deve Gowda, and wait for tensions between Congress and the United Front to build before pressing for new polls.
